statement: To an apotome only one rational straight line can be annexed which is commensurable with the whole in square only.
heath_proof: Let AB be an apotome, and BC an annex to it; therefore AC, CB are rational straight lines commensurable in square only. [X. 73] I say that no other rational straight line can be annexed to AB which is commensurable with the whole in square only. For, if possible, let BD be so annexed; therefore AD, DB are also rational straight lines commensurable in square only. [X. 73] Now, since the excess of the squares on AD, DB over twice the rectangle AD, DB is also the excess of the squares on AC, CB over twice the rectangle AC, CB, for both exceed by the same, the square on AB, [II. 7] therefore, alternately, the excess of the squares on AD, DB over the squares on AC, CB is the excess of twice the rectangle AD, DB over twice the rectangle AC, CB. But the squares on AD, DB exceed the squares on AC, CB by a rational area, for both are rational; therefore twice the rectangle AD, DB also exceeds twice the rectangle AC, CB by a rational area: which is impossible, for both are medial [X. 21], and a medial area does not exceed a medial by a rational area. [X. 26] Therefore no other rational straight line can be annexed to AB which is commensurable with the whole in square only. Therefore only one rational straight line can be annexed to an apotome which is commensurable with the whole in square only.

10.79
**Statement:** To an apotome only one rational straight line can be annexed which is commensurable with the whole in square only.

**Step 1.** Let AB be an apotome, and let BC be the annex to it: C lies on AB produced beyond B, AC is a rational straight line, CB is a rational straight line commensurable with AC in square only, and AB is the remainder when CB is subtracted from AC [10.73]. Let ρ denote the assigned rational straight line, so that every rational straight line is commensurable with ρ in length or in square only, and in either case its square is commensurable with the square on ρ [D10.1.3]; such areas are rational [D10.1.4].

**Step 2.** Suppose, if possible, that a second rational straight line BD, different from BC, can be annexed to AB so as to be commensurable with the whole AD in square only. Since DB is rational, the square on DB is commensurable with the square on ρ; since AD is commensurable in square with DB, the square on AD is commensurable with the square on DB; hence the square on AD is commensurable with the square on ρ [10.12], so AD is rational [D10.1.3]. Thus AD, DB are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, and AB is the apotome obtained by subtracting DB from AD [10.73].

**Step 3.** The points C and D both lie on AB produced beyond B and are distinct, so one of BC, BD is the greater; let BD be the greater (if BC is the greater, interchange the letters C and D throughout). Then C lies between B and D, so that AC is a part of AD and BC a part of BD; therefore AD is greater than AC and DB is greater than CB [CN5]. Consequently the square on AC is a part of the square on AD and the square on CB a part of the square on DB, so the squares on AD, DB together exceed the squares on AC, CB together [CN5]. Let the excess be the area E, so that the squares on AD, DB together are equal to the squares on AC, CB together with E.

**Step 4.** The straight line AC is cut at B; therefore the squares on AC, CB together are equal to twice the rectangle AC, CB together with the square on AB [2.7]. Likewise the straight line AD is cut at B; therefore the squares on AD, DB together are equal to twice the rectangle AD, DB together with the square on AB [2.7].

**Step 5.** Substituting the equalities of Step 4 into the equality of Step 3, twice the rectangle AD, DB together with the square on AB is equal to twice the rectangle AC, CB together with the square on AB and with E [CN1]. Subtracting the square on AB from both, twice the rectangle AD, DB is equal to twice the rectangle AC, CB together with E [CN3]. That is, twice the rectangle AD, DB exceeds twice the rectangle AC, CB by the area E.

**Step 6.** The area E is rational. For AD, DB, AC, CB are rational straight lines, so the squares on them are each commensurable with the square on ρ [D10.1.3] and are therefore rational [D10.1.4] and commensurable with one another [10.12]. The squares on AD, DB being commensurable, their sum is commensurable with the square on AD [10.15], hence with the square on ρ [10.12]; likewise the sum of the squares on AC, CB is commensurable with the square on ρ. These two sums, being each commensurable with the square on ρ, are commensurable with one another [10.12]. Now the greater sum (the squares on AD, DB) is composed of the lesser sum (the squares on AC, CB) and E, and the whole is commensurable with the part consisting of the lesser sum; therefore the lesser sum and E are commensurable [10.15]. Hence E is commensurable with the square on ρ [10.12], that is, E is rational [D10.1.4].

**Step 7.** Twice the rectangle AD, DB is medial. For AD, DB are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, so the rectangle AD, DB is medial [10.21]. Twice this rectangle has to the rectangle the ratio which the number 2 has to the number 1, so it is commensurable with the rectangle [10.6]; and an area commensurable with a medial area is medial [10.23, Porism]. Therefore twice the rectangle AD, DB is medial. In the same way, since AC, CB are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, the rectangle AC, CB is medial [10.21], and twice it, being commensurable with it [10.6], is medial [10.23, Porism].

**Step 8.** By Steps 5, 6 and 7, the medial area twice the rectangle AD, DB exceeds the medial area twice the rectangle AC, CB by the rational area E. But a medial area does not exceed a medial area by a rational area [10.26]. This is impossible.

**Step 9.** Therefore the supposition of Step 2 is false: no rational straight line other than BC can be annexed to the apotome AB so as to be commensurable with the whole in square only. Hence to an apotome only one rational straight line can be annexed which is commensurable with the whole in square only. Q.E.D.
